article_title: SIPPS (Systematic Instruction in Phonological Awareness, Phonics, and Sight Words)
citation: SIPPS program description and outcomes review. (2022). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/
title: Use placement and embedded mastery tests to drive grouping, pacing, and reteaching decisions
description: The article describes an assessment system in which "Assessment data determines placement in the program" and flexible groups based on placement results provide differentiated instruction. Criterion-referenced mastery tests embedded at designated intervals document mastery of phonics and high-frequency words and "support instructional decisions to guide reteaching, which may include adjusting pacing and delivery." This keeps instruction matched to individual progress through an accelerative scope and sequence.
requirements: Initial and ongoing assessment; criterion-referenced mastery tests embedded at designated intervals in each level's scope and sequence
target_learners: K-12 students in differentiated small groups within a foundational reading program
target_learning_goals: Efficient progression through foundational reading skills matched to individual need
examples: Students in the evaluation were placed at points of need within a level and lesson, with progress monitoring used throughout
key_sources: SIPPS program description and outcomes review. (2022). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/

article_title: Statistical Power for School-Based RCTs with Binary Outcomes
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2013). Statistical Power for School-Based RCTs with Binary Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 6, issue 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/statistical-power-for-school-based-rcts-with-binary-outcomes
title: Plan larger school samples when designing clustered education RCTs with binary outcomes
description: Because binary outcomes demand larger samples than continuous test-score or behavioral-scale outcomes, designers of clustered school-based RCTs should plan for more schools than the 40 to 60 typically used. The article's key finding is that "sample sizes of 40 to 60 schools that are typically included in clustered RCTs for student test score or behavioral scale outcomes will often be insufficient for binary outcomes," so power calculations should use the article's logit-based approach.
requirements: Power planning must be conducted before the trial using the logit-based sample size formulas for the planned binary outcome
constraints: Applies to clustered designs with school- or teacher-level random assignment and binary outcomes
target_learners: K-12 students in school-based intervention studies
target_learning_goals: Adequately powered education RCTs measuring binary outcomes
examples: The article derives sample size formulas for clustered designs using generalized estimating equation methods to support this planning
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2013). Statistical Power for School-Based RCTs with Binary Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 6, issue 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/statistical-power-for-schoolbased-rcts-with-binary-outcomes

article_title: Technical Methods Report: Statistical Power for Regression Discontinuity Designs in Education Evaluations
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). Technical Methods Report: Statistical Power for Regression Discontinuity Designs in Education Evaluations. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov
title: Plan evaluation sample sizes around the larger requirements of clustered RD designs before choosing between RD and experimental designs
description: Because clustered RD designs typically demand substantially larger samples than clustered experiments for equivalent statistical precision, evaluators should assess power implications before committing to an RD design. The report finds that "three to four times larger samples are typically required under RD than experimental clustered designs to produce impacts with the same level of statistical precision." This principle directs researchers to weigh that power cost against RD's applicability when the assignment point, pretests, and research questions make RD feasible.
requirements: Sufficient sample size at the cutoff to offset the power disadvantage relative to a clustered experimental design
constraints: Viability depends on the point of treatment assignment, the availability of pretests, and key research questions, and may be limited for new impact evaluations of educational interventions
target_learners: Students in education evaluations using clustered RD designs
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of intervention effects on student test scores
examples: The report's empirical work focuses on commonly used designs in education research testing intervention effects on student test scores under clustered RD designs
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). Technical Methods Report: Statistical Power for Regression Discontinuity Designs in Education Evaluations. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/technical-methods-report-statistical-power-for-regression-discontinuity-designs-in-education-evaluations

article_title: Expected and Emerging Requirements for Digital Learning Platforms as Research Infrastructure
citation: Roschelle, J., Wortman, A., & Pautz Stephenson, S. (2025, January). Expected and Emerging Requirements for Digital Learning Platforms as Research Infrastructure. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/241
title: Platform-specific content authoring pathways let researchers run A/B tests on curricular variations within each platform's structure
description: Each SEERNet platform gives researchers a distinct way to author or modify content for comparative experiments, matched to the platform's architecture. E-TRIALS can randomize new versus existing presentations of mathematical symbols; Terracotta works with any content entered into the Canvas LMS, letting researchers test alternative versions of assigned content; OpenStax Kinetic lets researchers create Qualtrics surveys or interventional activities students access from Kinetic dashboards, with Qualtrics chosen because many learning scientists already use it. E-TRIALS also supports conditional assignment based on student responses, enabling evaluation focused on students who could most benefit.
requirements: Platform tools that preserve randomization and single-factor variation; E-TRIALS monitors studies to ensure supports vary by a single factor
constraints: Platform scope limits apply: OpenStax Kinetic supports changes in labs but not in its core textbooks, and some content is blocked by school firewalls, which E-TRIALS works around via the ASSISTments YouTube channel
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students on the platforms
target_learning_goals: testing whether modified curricular supports increase learning via A/B experiments
examples: Dr. Avery Closser's SEERNet study adjusts how symbolic math is presented to help students visualize expression structure via E-TRIALS randomization
key_sources: Roschelle, J., Wortman, A., & Pautz Stephenson, S. (2025, January). Expected and Emerging Requirements for Digital Learning Platforms as Research Infrastructure. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/241

article_title: Continuous Improvement and Postsecondary Student Success
citation: Barbara Means and Julie Neisler. (2004). Continuous Improvement for Student Success. Digital Promise Global. https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2004/12/06/the-bell-curve
title: Plan comparison groups and data sources in advance, because rigorous courseware impact studies require comparable treatment and comparison groups and cannot be left to busy developers or faculty alone.
description: The article distills lessons from the NGCC evaluation about conducting impact studies: measuring impact requires an objective outcome measure, a comparison group, evidence of comparability, adequate numbers in both groups, and holding other influences constant. It warns that "Comparison groups and data sources need to be planned in advance if you want to get an apples-to-apples comparison of different versions of a course." It also cautions that busy technology developers, marketers, or faculty cannot be expected to design and execute rigorous impact studies without considerable help.
requirements: An objective and consistent outcome measure, a comparison group, evidence the groups are comparable, adequate numbers in both groups, and other potential influences held constant.
constraints: Strong traditions of faculty independence around learning goals, instructional approach, assessment and grading practices impede efforts to learn what works best.
target_learners: Higher education students in courseware-supported courses
target_learning_goals: Improving course outcomes and measuring the impact of digital courseware redesigns
examples: In the NGCC evaluation, 77 impact data sets were submitted but only 28 had adequate numbers of reasonably comparable students in the two conditions.
key_sources: Barbara Means and Julie Neisler. (2004). Continuous Improvement for Student Success. Digital Promise Global. https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2004/12/06/the-bell-curve

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — The UX Design Loop
citation: Gartrell, J. and Johnson, E. (2026). ATS Field Note: The UX Design Loop. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/299
title: Plan UX research backwards from the product decisions you need to make
description: The article recommends planning research "backwards": "start with the product decisions you'll need to make and work back to what you need to learn in order to make those decisions." This keeps studies focused on decision-relevant learning rather than producing "interesting but inconclusive findings." It is operationalized in Phase 1 of the Design Loop, where teams align on decisions, learning needs, and how to learn them.
requirements: Teams must first identify the key product decisions at stake before selecting research methods
target_learners: education R&D and product teams
examples: The resource 'UX Research Studies that Get Results' explains planning user research backwards from product decisions
key_sources: Gartrell, J. and Johnson, E. (2026). ATS Field Note: The UX Design Loop. In ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/299

article_title: Promise Neighborhoods Case Studies
citation: Hulsey, L., Esposito, A. M., Boller, K., & Osborn, S. (2015). Promise Neighborhoods Case Studies (Issue Brief). Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Place-based grantee-led implementation of community support programs for children in poverty
description: Promise Neighborhoods are implemented locally by lead agencies that receive federal funding and choose which services to offer their community. The pattern pairs flexible, locally selected services with a common cradle-to-career goal; case studies documented "the services they chose to offer, and the early successes and challenges they had in improving the lives of children in their community."
requirements: A local lead agency authorized to design and select services for its community
constraints: The article describes sites as being in the early implementation stage of a long-term endeavor
target_learners: Children and families in high-poverty Promise Neighborhoods communities
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive educational and developmental support across childhood
examples: Five case-study sites were selected from among 48 lead agencies funded across 23 states and the District of Columbia

article_title: Equity-Focused Schools Carry All Students to High Levels
citation: Equity-focused Schools Carry All Students to High Levels. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://www.wested.org
title: Professional learning communities (PLCs) with team structures and weekly scheduled meetings
description: Professional learning communities are structures that help educators inquire about and solve problems and reflect on their work together. In all four case study schools, staff studied the PLC concept, built common understanding, and carried it out with fidelity. Montgomery Center used PLCs to introduce team-level analysis of curriculum, instruction, and assessment, and created an Academic Student Support Team to track the impact of student interventions over time. All case schools have grade-level or multigrade teams, vertical teams to align curriculum across grades, team leaders, and scheduled meetings of at least an hour a week, and most also have data teams.
requirements: Scheduled team meeting times of at least an hour a week
A common studied understanding of the PLC concept implemented with fidelity
target_learners: teachers and other educators in K-12 public schools
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of instruction through collaborative inquiry and data use
examples: Montgomery Center School created grade-level PLCs, a middle school PLC, and an Academic Student Support Team tracking intervention impacts over time.

article_title: STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis
citation: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm
title: Three-component definition of a professional learning community with an inclusive STEM operating threshold
description: The synthesis defines a PLC through its three constituent components, each of which must be fulfilled for an activity to count: "professional – engaging educators in the development of their professional practice; learning – focused on both the learning of the educators and the learning of their students; and community – which requires common vision, goals, purpose, and a shared sense of trust". Operationally the study used an inclusive rather than restrictive threshold: groups of three or more teachers with a STEM focus, sustained rather than one-shot, excluding whole-school PLCs and two-person interactions such as mentoring pairs. This framework governed which studies were included and anchors the synthesis's design guidance.
requirements: Each component in the term Professional Learning Community — professional, learning, and community — should be fulfilled in order to regard some activity as a PLC.
constraints: The study's STEM focus precluded consideration of enterprises where whole schools are operating as PLCs, and collaborative work by two teachers, such as a single mentor-new-teacher induction pairing, was excluded.
target_learners: K-12 STEM teachers
preservice STEM teachers
examples: Panelists questioned whether a thin lesson study enterprise should count as a PLC, worrying that including low-level endeavors with limited effects would make the PLC reputation that of a fad.
key_sources: Fulton, K., Doerr, H., & Britton, T. (2010). STEM Teachers in Professional Learning Communities: A Knowledge Synthesis. National Commission on Teaching & America's Future / WestEd. https://www.nctaf.org/resources/events/STEMWingspreadConference.htm

article_title: Educating for Equity: Alder Graduate School's Teacher Residency
citation: Yun, C., Fitz, J., Nakajima, T., & Mauerman, C. (2025). Educating for equity: Alder Graduate School's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/812.965
title: Coursework aligned to four Program Learning Outcomes integrated across all courses
description: Alder's curriculum is organized around four Program Learning Outcomes: asset-based community and cultural responsiveness; developmentally appropriate, whole child, and inclusive practices; pedagogical content knowledge; and critical, reflective, and research-based orientations to teaching. The report states that "The integration of these PLOs into each course allowed residents to see and experience similar concepts across courses, which helped reinforce learning and encouraged residents to reflect on their clinical experiences in relation to the PLOs throughout the residency year."
requirements: Course objectives and content aligned to the PLOs across all credential pathways, with courses sequenced across summer, fall, and spring terms
target_learners: Teacher residency candidates in Multiple Subject, Single Subject, and Education Specialist pathways
target_learning_goals: Equity-oriented, whole child, and reflective teaching practice grounded in pedagogical content knowledge
examples: Course assessments asked residents to pull in details of their specific clinical contexts and apply theory to analyze their experiences
key_sources: Yun, C., Fitz, J., Nakajima, T., & Mauerman, C. (2025). Educating for equity: Alder Graduate School's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/812.965

article_title: Designing faculty standards for technology integration in higher education institutions: a design-based research study
citation: Helen Crompton, Diane Burke and Christine Nickel. (2026). Designing faculty standards for technology integration in higher education institutions: a design-based research study. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00584-y
title: Write standards language plainly and in task order so faculty can read indicators with the meaning intended
description: During macro cycle one, participants requested simplifying complicated words such as leverage to use, removing redundant or synonymous words, and ordering indicators in the sequence they happen in practice, from design to facilitate and then to evaluate. The authors argue reducing complexity matters because educators can lack self-efficacy in integrating technology and reading comprehension is highly tied to background knowledge, so connecting to what faculty already know makes the indicators easier to follow.
requirements: Indicator wording should be checked with the intended faculty audience for clarity, word order, and missing components
constraints: The article grounds this in feedback from its participant groups; it does not claim generalizability beyond standards documents of this kind
target_learners: Higher education faculty reading and applying the standards
target_learning_goals: Accessible interpretation of technology integration standards and indicators
examples: The word leverage was swapped to use, plan and teach were removed as synonymous with design and facilitate, and indicators were aligned with the task order for the standard
key_sources: Helen Crompton, Diane Burke and Christine Nickel. (2026). Designing faculty standards for technology integration in higher education institutions: a design-based research study. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00584-y

article_title: Beyond the AI Tutor: Social Learning with LLM Agents
citation: Harsh Kumar, Zi Kang (Jace) Mu, Jonathan Vincentius, Ashton Anderson. (2026). Human Thinking under Plural LLM Assistance: Mathematical Problem Solving and Open-Ended Writing. Working Paper, July 2026, Toronto, Canada. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02677
title: Plural LLM assistance as a configurable arrangement of support around the user
description: This framework treats LLM assistance as a design space defined by arrangement rather than only by model capability or response quality. As the article puts it, "LLM assistance can vary not only in model capability or response quality, but also in how support is arranged, e.g., one voice or many, one model or several, generalist or specialist roles". The framework holds that roles and personas are interfaces and prompting choices rather than human-like social actors, and that arrangement affects performance, confidence, and diversity of thought. The two experiments instantiate this space with tutor/peer arrangements in math and single-versus-role-specialized-duo arrangements in writing.
requirements: LLM agents instantiated with distinct system prompts defining roles, with learners introduced to each agent's strengths and tendencies so they can calibrate trust
constraints: The explored design space is deliberately narrow: agent count, error types, role specializations, and interaction structure were held largely constant, and the experiments are a first step rather than a definitive map
target_learners: adult crowdworkers solving math problems or writing essays
target_learning_goals: open-ended argumentative and creative writing quality and idea diversity
examples: Experiment-1 compared Control, Peers Only, Tutor Only, and Tutor + Peers support conditions during lesson phases, then measured unassisted test accuracy on isomorphic problems.
Experiment-2 compared no AI, a single generalist assistant, and a pair of role-specialized assistants (Claude and ChatGPT with complementary roles) for argumentative and creative essay writing.
key_sources: Harsh Kumar, Zi Kang (Jace) Mu, Jonathan Vincentius, Ashton Anderson. (2026). Human Thinking under Plural LLM Assistance: Mathematical Problem Solving and Open-Ended Writing. Working Paper, July 2026, Toronto, Canada. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02677

article_title: Professional Learning Communities: A Review of the Literature
citation: Stoll, L., Bolam, R., McMahon, A., Wallace, M., & Thomas, S. (2006). Professional Learning Communities: A Review of the Literature. Journal of Educational Change. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10833-006-0001-8
title: Professional learning communities as a vehicle for capacity building and sustainable school improvement
description: The review positions professional learning communities (PLCs) as an organisational approach to school improvement: "Developing professional learning communities appears to hold considerable promise for capacity building for sustainable improvement." It notes that PLCs have "become a 'hot topic' in many countries," indicating wide international policy and practice interest. The framework connects teacher learning communities to the capacity blend of motivation, skill, organisational conditions and support infrastructure described elsewhere in the review.
requirements: Developing PLCs requires sustained attention to the organisational conditions and support infrastructure that constitute capacity
constraints: The promise is stated with hedging ('appears to hold considerable promise'), not as a demonstrated effect
target_learners: teachers
school leaders
key_sources: Stoll, L., Bolam, R., McMahon, A., Wallace, M., & Thomas, S. (2006). Professional Learning Communities: A Review of the Literature. Journal of Educational Change. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10833-006-0001-8

article_title: A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools
citation: Li, S., Zeng, C., Liu, H., Jia, J., Liang, M., Cha, Y., Lim, C. P., & Wu, X. (2025). A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00566-y
title: Adapted Personalized Learning Continuum Framework (PLCF) for categorizing AI-enabled personalized learning models
description: The article adapts the Personalized Learning Continuum Framework of Lokey-Vega and Stephens (2019) as an analytical lens for classifying AI-enabled personalized learning models along the proportion of Academic Learning Time spent on automated versus student-centered pedagogies and the distribution of power and agency. Model A is "fully automated, with 100% of ALT delivered through an adaptive platform and minimal teacher or peer involvement"; Model B is a balanced hybrid; Model C is learner-driven with 80% collaborative, project-based learning. The framework served as the coding scheme for the learning-model-type moderator in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Studies must be codable by proportion of Academic Learning Time on automated versus student-centered pedagogies and by distribution of power among teachers, students, and technologies
constraints: The article notes the PLCF has acknowledged conceptual limitations (citing Lively, 2023) and that the framework was adapted to fit the scope of the analysis
target_learners: K-12 students in STEM subjects
target_learning_goals: Personalized STEM learning across knowledge, skills, engagement, and attitudes
examples: The meta-analysis coded included RCTs into Models A, B, and C and found Model C (g = 0.764) more effective than Model A (g = 0.257)
key_sources: Li, S., Zeng, C., Liu, H., Jia, J., Liang, M., Cha, Y., Lim, C. P., & Wu, X. (2025). A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00566-y

article_title: Modelling the long-run learning impact of the Covid-19 learning shock: Actions to (more than) mitigate loss
citation: Kaffenberger, Michelle. (2021). Modelling the long-run learning impact of the Covid-19 learning shock: Actions to (more than) mitigate loss. International Journal of Educational Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijedudev.2020.102326
title: Plan remediation on reopening and build it into lasting reorientation of instruction to children's learning levels
description: The article recommends that systems begin planning remedial programmes immediately, and that while doing so they "build programmes and train teachers in ways that can continue to produce benefits beyond the period immediately following reopening". Remediation requires formative assessment of children's levels and teacher empowerment to adapt instruction; maintaining these practices — ongoing formative assessment, curriculum adjustment, and coaching or structured pedagogy support — is what turns a recovery programme into a 'build back better' scenario that surpasses pre-shock learning.
requirements: Formative assessments to identify children's learning levels on return
Teacher training and professional development, with teachers allowed and empowered to adapt the curriculum
constraints: The exact form must take each system's context, existing capabilities and constraints into account
target_learners: Children returning to school after Covid-19 closures, especially primary-grade cohorts in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: Catch-up on foundational skills and sustained learning gains through later grades
examples: The modelled remediation scenario covered the missed third of the grade 3 curriculum during grade 4 before resuming the normal pace; the reorientation scenario used an optimised pace of 35, a 22 percent reduction from 45
key_sources: Kaffenberger, Michelle. (2021). Modelling the long-run learning impact of the Covid-19 learning shock: Actions to (more than) mitigate loss. International Journal of Educational Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijedudev.2020.102326

article_title: Casual Games, Cognition, and Play across the Lifespan: A Critical Synthesis
citation: Kurt Squire, Garrison Wells, Maria J. Anderson-Coto, and Constance Steinkuehler. 2023. Casual Games, Cognition, and Play across the Lifespan: A Critical Synthesis. ACM Games: Research and Practice, Volume 1, Issue 2, Article 14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3594534
title: Play as an emergent phenomenon of person, intention, game, and context — the unit of analysis for game-based learning research
description: This framework holds that the effects of casual games arise not from the media artifact itself but from play as an emergent phenomenon at the intersection of people, their intentions, the game, and context. The review argues researchers "should take seriously the context of game play, perhaps treating the emergent phenomena of play as the unit of analysis, rather than the media artifact." It draws on the mindset literature, noting that intention and expectation shape outcomes, so the same game can benefit or harm the same players in different contexts.
requirements: Research designs must account for players' motivations, intentions, and the social context of play when evaluating game impact.
constraints: The review treats casual games as a media type rather than a frame of mind for consistency with the existing research literature, while noting future studies may benefit from examining the activity instead.
target_learners: players across the lifespan, including older adults and youth
examples: The review's Pokémon Go synthesis shows users who play for social reasons report positive well-being while those playing for escapism or nostalgia report less positive well-being.
key_sources: Kurt Squire, Garrison Wells, Maria J. Anderson-Coto, and Constance Steinkuehler. 2023. Casual Games, Cognition, and Play across the Lifespan: A Critical Synthesis. ACM Games: Research and Practice, Volume 1, Issue 2, Article 14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3594534

article_title: Planning prompts increase and forecast course completion in massive open online courses
citation: Yeomans, Michael and Reich, Justin. 2017. "Planning Prompts Increase and Forecast Course Completion in Massive Open Online Courses." Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). https://doi.org/10.1145/3027385.3027416
title: Deliver open-ended planning prompts at the outset of a learning experience to encourage follow-through
description: Because most MOOC learners who intend to complete fail to do so, the article recommends plan-making as a low-cost intervention: "plan-making is a cheap and effective nudge to encourage follow-through." In practice, instructors present open-ended planning prompts at the beginning of a course, asking learners to write plans whose content can also serve as an early signal of risk. The article reports this raised completion by 29% and certificate payment by 40% in three HarvardX courses.
requirements: Prompts are open-ended and delivered at the beginning of the course, before goal pursuit begins.
constraints: The effect was largest for students enrolled in traditional schools, so benefits may vary across learner subgroups.
target_learners: MOOC learners intending to complete a course
examples: Students in three HarvardX courses received open-ended planning prompts at the beginning of a course in a natural field experiment.
key_sources: Yeomans, Michael and Reich, Justin. 2017. "Planning Prompts Increase and Forecast Course Completion in Massive Open Online Courses." Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). https://doi.org/10.1145/3027385.3027416

article_title: Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy
citation: Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, Stefanie Meliss. (2026). Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09779-2
title: Pluralistic theoretical framework of modelling drawing on practice-based, social learning and cognitive theories
description: The article organises its hypotheses through a framework combining three traditions. Practice Based Teacher Education theorises that representations of practice help pre-service teachers notice important features of teaching; Bandura’s social learning theory holds that observation builds skills and self-efficacy; cognitive theory holds that models encode information more efficiently than verbal descriptions. The article states: “This research adopts a pluralistic theoretical approach, drawing on the practice-based, social learning and cognitive theories of modelling to develop a number of hypotheses”. The simulator experiment then tests hypotheses derived from each strand.
requirements: Models must make observable examples of the focal practice available to trainees, whether live or symbolic (video)
constraints: The skill finding supports the framework’s skill predictions, but the knowledge and self-efficacy predictions were not supported in this teacher-education domain
target_learners: pre-service (initial) teacher trainees
target_learning_goals: skill in using evidence-based teaching practices (questioning for retrieval)
examples: Hypotheses 1–4 were derived respectively from cognitive/worked-example theory, feature-highlighting theory, procedural–conceptual integration, and Bandura’s vicarious modelling
key_sources: Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, Stefanie Meliss. (2026). Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09779-2

article_title: Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model
citation: Tillema, M., van den Bergh, H., Rijlaarsdam, G., & Sanders, T. (2011). Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9072-x
title: Planner and reviser writing styles as temporally distinct configurations of (meta)cognitive activities
description: The article works within a temporal model of writing in which the quality of task execution depends on when (meta)cognitive activities occur, not only how often. Within it, two extreme styles are defined: "Planners are writers who generate plans before text production. Revisers use text production as a means to arrive at a content plan." The styles imply different temporal distributions of activities such as reading the assignment, planning, text production and revising, and are measured as continuous dimensions rather than categories.
requirements: Measurement of writing behaviour must capture the moments at which activities occur, since the styles are defined by temporal distribution across task execution.
constraints: The article raises doubts about the usability of the reviser dimension for less proficient writers, given its lower reliability and the extreme low frequency of revising activities in this age group.
target_learners: secondary school students (fourteen- and fifteen-year-olds) writing argumentative essays
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing processes, including planning, text production and revising
examples: Students with higher planner scores applied more planning activities at the start of task execution, fitting the planner style definition.
key_sources: Tillema, M., van den Bergh, H., Rijlaarsdam, G., & Sanders, T. (2011). Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9072-x

article_title: Playful Study Design: A Novel Approach to Enhancing Student Well-Being and Academic Performance
citation: Costantini, A., Bakker, A. B., & Scharp, Y. S. (2025). Playful Study Design: A Novel Approach to Enhancing Student Well-Being and Academic Performance. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10022-6
title: Playful study design: a student-driven, two-dimensional construct of ludic (fun) and agonistic (competitive) play applied to academic tasks
description: The article defines PSD as "a proactive cognitive-behavioral approach that students use to infuse their academic tasks with enjoyment and challenge," positioning the student as the designer who creates the study experience. It comprises two dimensions mapped onto play theory: ludic play, involving "lightheartedness, humor, and imagination," and agonistic play, focused on "challenge, competition, and personal achievement." Unlike top-down gamification, PSD emphasizes self-initiated play integrated into study routines, and is distinguished from deliberate practice because it treats play as an approach to activities rather than an activity itself.
requirements: Students must have discretion over how they approach their study tasks, since PSD is defined as self-initiated and student-driven rather than instructor-imposed.
constraints: The article develops and tests PSD in university settings; the authors note structured, top-down play approaches can even backfire, citing a gamified course in which students felt less motivated over time.
target_learners: university students in higher education
examples: Students may introduce fun by using humor, creating imaginative study tools, or developing engaging narratives, and may incorporate competition by setting personal goals, engaging in friendly competition with peers, or striving to surpass previous performance.

article_title: On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging
citation: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2
title: Place-belongingness and politics of belonging framework for student belonging in higher education
description: The framework characterizes belonging both as an intimate personal feeling of 'being at home' and as tied to social forces that include and exclude. It specifies six factors of place-belongingness—auto-biographical, relational, cultural, economic, legal, and elective—and holds that these must be read against structures of power that delineate who gets to belong. The article applies it to universities, arguing that systems of whiteness and intersecting oppression shape students' diverse constellations of belonging needs.
requirements: Analysis must attend to both the personal feeling of belonging and the power structures that afford or constrain it
constraints: The framework theorizes broadly around migration, nationalism, and citizenship, and its higher-education application is attributed to Covarrubias (2023)
target_learners: low-income, first-generation-to-college students of color in higher education
target_learning_goals: fostering students' sense of belonging and acceptance in university settings
examples: The article uses the framework to organize its review of harmful and transformative institutional acceptance practices and to analyze how scripts of multiculturalism and exceptionalism erase relational, legal, and economic belonging needs

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno
citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: The edited volume Cognitive Load Theory (Plass, Moreno, & Brünken, 2010) and its involved coherence review process
description: This element is the edited volume Cognitive Load Theory, published in 2010 by Cambridge University Press and edited by Plass, Moreno, and Brünken. Plass's tribute describes the very involved review process implemented for the 12 chapters of the book, aimed at assuring the coherence and quality of the individual contributions. He acknowledges that the editing process and resulting revisions delayed publication, but reports that the rigor of the process was justified by the resulting strength of the chapters by all contributing authors.
requirements: The volume comprised 12 chapters that were subjected to an involved review process to assure coherence and quality across contributions
constraints: The editing process and resulting revisions delayed the book's publication, and some authors were not used to this level of editing
target_learners: educational psychology researchers and scholars engaging with cognitive load theory
target_learning_goals: understanding cognitive load theory and its applications to instruction
examples: Plass, Moreno, and Brünken edited the volume together, with Moreno contributing the coherence-oriented review process for its chapters

article_title: A domain-specific perspective on adaptivity
citation: Anselm Strohmaier, Fien Depaepe, Michael Nickl, Andreas Obersteiner. (2026). A domain-specific perspective on adaptivity. Learning and Instruction 104. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102364
title: Plass and Pawar's three-dimension framework of adaptive support
description: The editorial adopts Plass and Pawar's (2020) conceptualization, in which adaptive support is organized around three questions: which learner variables to adapt for, how these variables can be reliably measured, and what adaptations can be made during learning. The authors state that Plass and Pawar (2020) "conceptualize adaptive support through three dimensions" and use this structure to analyze where domain-specificity matters in each dimension, since these dimensions are also apparent in most other adaptivity frameworks.
requirements: Interpretation of process data depends on theoretical frameworks that link observable behavior to cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms within a domain
constraints: Without this interpretive bridge, more data do not necessarily yield better adaptation.
target_learners: learners in technology-supported adaptive learning environments
target_learning_goals: tailoring instruction to individual learner needs to enhance learning outcomes
examples: The editorial structures its synthesis of the special issue's nine studies and one discussion paper around the three dimensions: variables to adapt for, measurement, and instructional response.

article_title: The education and control of the emotions.
citation: Henry, T. S. (1916). The Education and Control of the Emotions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Reward desired emotional expression with pleasure and attach unpleasant consequences to harmful emotions
description: A general rule for teachers developing good emotions: provide every opportunity for desirable emotions to originate, then ensure their proper expression is 'rewarded with pleasure, so that a definite connection may be set up between the emotional state and the pleasurable consequences'. Conversely, situations calling forth harmful emotions should be avoided and unpleasant consequences connected with their expression. The article presents this as the application of consequence experience to emotional life.
requirements: Opportunities for the desired emotion to originate must be provided so that pleasurable consequences can be connected with its proper expression
constraints: The article frames the rule as an application of Spencer's 'doctrine of natural punishments', relying on experience with natural individual and social consequences rather than teacher-imposed rewards alone
target_learners: school children
examples: The article prescribes avoiding every situation which tends to call forth a harmful emotion and connecting unpleasant consequences with its expression, citing Thorndike's Principles of Teaching.

article_title: College marking systems.
citation: Kohl, C. C., & Hughes, P. (1911). Communications and discussions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology
title: Design instruction and student progress so that no student needs to fail
description: This principle holds that because a failure mark signals a student should not proceed without repeating work, instructors should not expect any fixed share of students to fail. Hughes argues that "under proper conditions no one would be invited to commence a term's work with the expectation that he must fail and repeat it," and that with attention to planning, admission, and progress-tracking it is often possible to insure that none shall fail.
requirements: Due attention to planning the work, admitting men to classes, and keeping track of their progress
constraints: The article concedes more men may be passed in some classes and fewer in others than believed should pass
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: successful completion of coursework without failure and repetition
examples: Hughes cites the Michigan Department of Literature, Science and the Arts, where failures remained below 3 per cent after adopting a standard ranking scale

article_title: Alleged elements of waste in learning a motor problem by the "part" method.
citation: Pechstein, L. A. (1917). Alleged Elements of Waste in Learning a Motor Problem by the "Part" Method. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Place association account of waste in part learning
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that mastering each maze unit establishes temporal and spatial positional relationships, locating each turn, cul de sac, and section relative to the time span, distance, the food-box, the starting place, and the experimenter. All waste in part learning "occurs in the act of connection and is here traceable almost entirely to the influence of place association," because connecting units demands breaking up these positional establishments.
requirements: Units must first be mastered as units, with positional establishments formed as necessary by-products of that mastery
constraints: The account is offered for the field of motor learning represented by the maze; the author waives a demonstrable comparison with rote learning
target_learners: college students learning motor tasks
examples: Behavior in the initial act of connection showed constant returning to the starting place, delay at closed exits, hesitation, confusion, and discouragement as runners vainly relied on short time and distance relationships

article_title: Grit and academic resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic
citation: Chen, D. L., Ertac, S., Evgeniou, T., Miao, X., Nadaf, A., & Yilmaz, E. (2024). Grit and academic resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00265-3
title: Use digital learning platform data to assess non-cognitive skills and customize learning experiences for students with heterogeneous resilience
description: Digital learning platforms can serve not only to deliver content but also to collect behavioral information that measures non-cognitive skills like grit and predicts responses to shocks. The article argues AI-based remote learning technologies can "identify not only students who are struggling in terms of comprehension but also those who lack resilience or motivation" and respond by adapting difficulty levels and sequences and providing personalized motivational feedback. Survey self-reports can be complemented with high-dimensional revealed-preference data.
requirements: A digital platform integrated into regular schooling that records behavioral activity such as clicks, content access, and time on task
constraints: The article's data cannot definitively infer causality; results may depend on how the pandemic was experienced and the platform's degree of curriculum integration
target_learners: K-12 students learning via digital platforms, including in remote-learning conditions
target_learning_goals: sustaining engagement and perseverance; academic resilience to disruptions
examples: Features promoting gritty behavior, such as growth-mindset messages, can be directly incorporated into digital learning environments to support self-regulated virtual learning

article_title: A methodological perspective on learning in the developing brain
citation: van Duijvenvoorde, A. C. K., Whitmore, L. B., Westhoff, B. & Mills, K. L. (2022). A methodological perspective on learning in the developing brain. npj Science of Learning 7:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00127-w
title: Three-fold taxonomy of brain plasticity: experience-independent, experience-expectant, and experience-dependent plasticity
description: The review organizes brain plasticity into three types: "experience-independent", in which brain changes unfold relatively independently of experience; "experience-expectant", in which neural sensitivity is attuned to particular environmental stimuli during specific developmental windows (sensitive periods); and "experience-dependent", which reflects individual-varying experiences and supports learning throughout life. The review grounds experience-expectant plasticity in ocular dominance work on the visual cortex and states that its discussion of learning focuses on experience-dependent learning across childhood and adolescence.
requirements: Relevant environmental input during sensitive periods for experience-expectant plasticity to unfold
constraints: The review's developmental cognitive neuroscience discussion focuses on experience-dependent learning rather than the other two types
target_learners: children
adolescents
target_learning_goals: understanding how experience shapes brain development and skill learning
examples: Depriving visual input to one eye produced ocular dominance in the visual cortex of the eye receiving input, demonstrating sensitive-period dependence of visual cortex development

article_title: Individual differences in frontoparietal plasticity in humans
citation: Boroshok, A. L., Park, A. T., Fotiadis, P., Velasquez, G. H., Tooley, U. A., Simon, K. R., Forde, J. C. P., Delgado Reyes, L. M., Tisdall, M. D., Bassett, D. S., Cooper, E. A. & Mackey, A. P. (2022). Individual differences in frontoparietal plasticity in humans. npj Science of Learning 7:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00130-1
title: Proxy measures of neural plasticity potential: VTA resting-state connectivity for dopamine system connectivity and T1w/T2w myelin maps for myelination
description: This framework treats neuroplasticity as a potential to change rather than a process, and operationalizes it in living humans with two MRI-based proxies. As the article states, "As a proxy for dopamine system connectivity, we analyzed resting-state functional connectivity between the VTA and task-active regions", drawing on animal work showing VTA stimulation enhances plasticity while myelination constrains it. Myelination is proxied by myelin map values, the ratio of T1-weighted to T2-weighted signal intensities in task-active regions. The framework predicts that stronger VTA-frontoparietal connectivity and lower myelin map values at baseline forecast greater learning from short-term training.
requirements: Baseline MRI scanning (structural T1w/T2w and resting-state fMRI) plus a task localizer to define task-active regions of interest before training begins
constraints: The article notes resting-state fMRI cannot distinguish top-down from bottom-up connectivity directions or dopamine from other transmission, and that only five minutes of resting-state data were collected, which may limit reliability
target_learners: healthy adults aged 18-25
target_learning_goals: predicting individual differences in learning gains from short-term cognitive training (working memory)
examples: In the study, five frontoparietal ROIs were identified with a 2-back > 1-back fMRI localizer contrast, and VTA rsFC and T1w/T2w ratios were extracted from each ROI to predict accuracy and response-time gains

article_title: WhatsApp Discourse Throughout COVID-19: Towards Computerized Evaluation of the Development of a STEM Teachers Professional Learning Community
citation: Zahava Scherz · Asaf Salman · Giora Alexandron · Yael Shwartz. (2023). WhatsApp Discourse Throughout COVID-19: Towards Computerized Evaluation of the Development of a STEM Teachers Professional Learning Community. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00320-3
title: A three-category coding scheme for assessing PLC WhatsApp discourse (Community Development, Knowledge Development, Administrative Issues)
description: The article synthesizes a coding scheme for assessing PLC discourse, built on teacher-knowledge frameworks (CK, PCK, TK) and PLC characteristics. It classifies each WhatsApp message into "three main categories": Community Development (building community, cooperation, sharing, positive feedback), Professional Knowledge Development (CK/PCK/TK and matching ASK- subcategories), and Administrative Issues, plus Media and Not Applicable tags. Messages are multi-labeled, discursive sequences are delimited into threads, and tags serve as indications of teachers' learning or PLC development.
requirements: Annotation by trained experts with joint training and consolidation sessions; validity requires both annotators agreeing on a tag (achieved IRR above 95%).
constraints: PK without content knowledge was not used as a separate category because the authors found it does not exist without content knowledge; Media tags were annotated automatically and excluded from reliability analysis.
target_learners: in-service STEM teacher leaders in professional learning communities
target_learning_goals: professional knowledge development (content, pedagogical-content, technological knowledge) and community development
examples: Example annotations include CK ('I checked with a physicist: the particles move by force of inertia...') and ASK-TK ('How do I assign students to separate zoom rooms?')

article_title: Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT
citation: Teo Susnjak. (2024). Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:452–482. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00336-3
title: Prescriptive Learning Analytics Framework (PLAF): an eight-step framework unifying predictive modelling, XAI transparency, and counterfactual prescriptive feedback
description: PLAF is a step-by-step framework with two key components, predictive and prescriptive phases, for identifying at-risk learners and generating evidence-based remedial advice. The article states that "The framework assumes that the data identification and acquisition steps have already been completed" and proceeds through feature engineering, model development, global interpretability (Step 4), local explainability (Step 5), counterfactual modelling (Step 6), natural-language conversion (Step 7), and intervention initiation (Step 8). It maps each step to specific technologies (SHAP, Anchors, DiCE, ChatGPT) and demonstrates practicality with use case scenarios on programme-completion prediction.
requirements: Data identification and acquisition steps must already be completed before the framework's steps begin
Counterfactual modelling must use actionable, mutable features constrained to feasible and realistic ranges
constraints: The framework was demonstrated on programme/qualification completion prediction at one Australasian HEI; the prescriptive phase's remaining evaluation is qualitative, using two hypothetical students
target_learners: at-risk undergraduate students at higher education institutions
target_learning_goals: timely identification of learners at risk of qualification non-completion and initiation of effective interventions
examples: The framework was demonstrated using programme/qualification completion predictive models built on a dataset of ~7000 learners, with two hypothetical-student case studies carried through the explainability and prescriptive steps

International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00231-1
title: Two-axis framework positioning online learning and hiring platforms by content-creator expertise and individuality of content-creation decisions
description: The article introduces a framework placing four online platforms along two axes: how much subject-matter expertise the average content creator has, and whether the content-creation decision is made individually or by groups/departments. Stack Overflow sits toward the novice/individual side, Udemy toward expert/small-team, and Stack Overflow Jobs at the extreme expert/group corner. The framework underpins the hypothesis that "more novice-driven and individual-driven platforms are more agile" in manifesting new topics.

constraints: Framework positions are approximate; the authors note the Google Trends placement "is not fully accurate"

lifelong learners in fast-changing professional domains

examples: Stack Overflow placed leaning toward novice side and entirely on individual-decision side; Stack Overflow Jobs placed at extreme upper right of the plane

citation: Pablo-César Muñoz-Carril, Nuria Hernández-Sellés, Eduardo-José Fuentes-Abeledo, Mercedes González-Sanmamed. (2021). Factors influencing students' perceived impact of learning and satisfaction in Computer Supported Collaborative Learning. Computers & Education, 174. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104310
title: Plan and monitor social interaction during CSCL design, since it does not arise spontaneously
description: The article holds that successful CSCL requires deliberately designing its social dimension: collaboration "must be planned in the design phase and monitored so that it happens properly during implementation". Designers should define social relationship aspects together with the cognitive aspects of task completion, foster a positive, socially accepting atmosphere, and attend to intra-group emotional support, motivation, and a sense of belonging to the community.
requirements: Detailed planning of pedagogical, curricular, social, and technological aspects before implementation
Teacher feedback and monitoring of interaction during implementation
constraints: The article warns that poor planning risks poor learning experiences and individual or group failures

examples: The studied courses required groups to agree on internal rules, member roles, communication tools, and how to act when a member was not committed to the task

article_title: The role of planning in complex problem solving
citation: Eichmann, B., Goldhammer, F., Greiff, S., Pucite, L., & Naumann, J. (2019). The role of planning in complex problem solving. Computers & Education, 128, 1-12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.08.004
title: Three behavioral process indicators for operationalizing planning in complex problem solving from log data
description: The article introduces three behavioral indicators extracted from computer-generated log data to operationalize planning in complex problem solving: "the duration of the longest interval between two successive interactions (duration indicator)", "the delay of the longest interval between two successive interactions from the beginning of the process (delay indicator)", and "the variance of times between each two successive interactions (variance indicator)". These indicators capture planning behavior occurring in the time between interactions, which the authors take to include understanding, representing, formulating, monitoring, and reflecting processes from the PISA framework.
requirements: Computer-based assessment tasks that generate log data recording the timing of each interaction with the task
constraints: The operationalization relies only on time between interactions, so it is not certain that students actually spent this time planning; students could have been reading the task or engaging in task-irrelevant behavior
target_learners: fifteen-year-old students in large-scale assessment

citation: Zha, Shenghua; Estes, Michele D.; and Xu, Ling. (2019). A meta-analysis on the effect of duration, task, and training in peer-led learning. Journal of Peer Learning, 12. https://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol12/iss1/2

It defines PLL as "a type of small group learning activity where student leaders, of similar status to the learners, guide or facilitate learning within a group." The framework is grounded in social learning, social identity, and social congruence theory, and was operationalised in a two-level random-effects meta-regression of 28 post-secondary studies.

constraints: The meta-analysis included only face-to-face post-secondary studies; online PLL was excluded
target_learners: Post-secondary undergraduate students

examples: Supplemental Instruction and Peer-Led Team Learning are named as widely adopted PLL program models that fit this framework

citation: Chumark, C. & Puncreobutr, V. (2016). Developing Basic Mathematical Skills of Pre-School Children by using Plasticized Clay. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(12). https://www.iiste.org

article_title: Effectiveness of Mobile Applications in Vocabulary Teaching
citation: Ahmet Basal, Selahattin Yilmaz, Asli Tanriverdi, & Lutfiye Sari. (2016). Effectiveness of Mobile Applications in Vocabulary Teaching. Contemporary Educational Technology, 7(1), 47-59. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/cet

citation: Andi Tenri Ampa. (2015). The Implementation of Interactive Multimedia Learning Materials in Teaching Listening Skills. English Language Teaching, 8(12). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n12p56
title: Four quality criteria for learning materials: relevance, consistency, practicality, effectiveness
description: The article adopts Plomp and Nieven's (2007) four points about the quality of learning materials: "relevance, consistency, practicality, and effectiveness". Relevance relates to the validity of the content; consistency refers to the validity of the construction; practicality is associated with the users of the products, here lecturers and students; and effectiveness refers to the achievement of expected outcomes. The article's preliminary studies addressed relevance, consistency and practicality, finding the products highly relevant, consistent, and practical, while the present study addressed effectiveness.
requirements: Evaluation of materials against all four quality points, with preliminary studies covering relevance, consistency and practicality before an effectiveness trial
target_learners: undergraduate students
examples: The article's preliminary studies by Ampa et al. (2015) concerned relevance, consistency, and practicality of the multimedia materials

citation: M. J. Wangila, W. Martin, M. Ronald. (2015). Effect of Programmed Instruction on Students' Attitude Towards Structure of the Atom and the Periodic Table among Kenyan Secondary Schools. Science Education International, Vol. 25, Issue 4, 488-500. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Science+Education+International
title: Programmed Learning Software (PLCD): a menu-driven CD-ROM for self-paced SAPT instruction
description: The Programmed Learning Software (PLS) was created by the researcher with a software engineer on a compact disk labelled "the PLCD" and served as the main teacher of the experimental groups. It is menu-driven, comprises 9 frames each covering one of the 9 sub-topics of SAPT, and each frame carries 6 icons: Lesson Objective, Content, Example, Quiz, Answer and Help. Learners progress at their own rate, answer quiz questions by keyboard or mouse, and the Help menu offers remedial options such as returning to a previous frame or easier examples. Experimental-group students received about 90% of their instruction via the PLCD during normal Chemistry lessons in computer laboratories, with the teacher only facilitating.

citation: Outi Kyrö-Ämmälä & Kaarina Määttä. (2011). Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n1p28
title: Keep play as a core part of primary-level teaching because it operates in the zone of proximal development
description: Drawing on Vygotsky and Dewey, the article argues that play belongs to children's world of ideas at primary level and that learning through playing builds a motivational basis for learning, since a child does not have to be persuaded to practise developing skills. "While playing, a child constantly acts on the area of the zone of proximal development", handling and assimilating new information in relation to prior experience with the help of others. Play is described as the most important prerequisite for developing a child's thoughts, will and feelings, which cannot be separated in play.
requirements: Understanding of play as a factor contributing to a child's development and supporting the child comprehensively
constraints: Schools' facilities and their book-oriented, decades-old learning structure often offer little opportunity for versatile play
target_learners: primary-level children transitioning from daycare and preschool
target_learning_goals: development of thoughts, will and feelings
examples: The article quotes Vygotsky's statement that 'a playing child towers over a child not playing'

title: Use online-platform learning data to target offline class time at students' weak skills
description: In this blended clinical skills course, teachers publish content online before class, monitor progress through platform data, and reshape offline sessions accordingly: for well-mastered skills students "practice independently", while weak areas receive emphasis, demonstration and focused practice instead of redundant lectures. Teachers able to adjust offline teaching content based on platform data

title: Empirical model of individual, parental, and institutional factors affecting mathematics education doctoral students' academic performance
description: A structural equation model in which five independent factors (fear of delay, student engagement, parental support, teacher support, and facilitating conditions) influence two intermediate factors (stress level and well-being), which along with the direct paths determine academic performance. The article states the model distinguished that five independent factors "can significantly influence two intermediated factors (namely stress level and well-being), and further influence the academic performance of mathematics education doctoral students". It was estimated with PLS-SEM on questionnaire data from 147 Indonesian doctoral students, with R2 of 0.651 for academic performance, 0.298 for stress level, and 0.592 for well-being, and nine of fourteen hypotheses supported.

constraints: Conclusions are based on a voluntary sample of mathematics education doctoral students in Indonesia, limiting generalizability to other higher education systems; only individual, institutional, and parental level variables were included

target_learning_goals: academic performance in doctoral coursework, research skills, and publication

title: Implement clinical registry work with planned implementation, shared responsibility, integration into daily routines and sufficient training
description: The article concludes that adding quality-register work to clinical care succeeds only when implementation is deliberately organised. examples: The study found that nurses created their own local systems to ensure patient follow-up and proper patient flow because formal routines, collaboration and teamwork were lacking.

university instructors

citation: Snyder JJ, Sloane JD, Dunk RDP, Wiles JR. (2016). Peer-Led Team Learning Helps Minority Students Succeed. PLoS Biology. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002398
title: Peer-Led Team Learning (PLTL) workshop model
description: PLTL is a well-defined active learning model in which students work in small groups of six to eight, led by an undergraduate peer leader who has successfully completed the same course. After training in group leadership methods, relevant learning theory, and course content, leaders work with an education specialist and the instructor to facilitate small group problem-solving. The article stresses that leaders "are not teachers. They are not tutors" and are not expected to provide answers; rather, they "help mentor students to actively construct their own understanding of concepts." Originally designed for undergraduate chemistry, it has been implemented in general biology, anatomy and physiology, and can be used alongside or in place of lecture.
requirements: Peer leaders must have successfully completed the same course their peer-team students are currently enrolled in
Peer leaders receive training in group leadership methods, relevant learning theory, and the conceptual content of the course
Leaders work collaboratively with an education specialist and the course instructor
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory STEM courses
target_learning_goals: student achievement and retention in STEM gatekeeper courses
examples: In the reported introductory biology course, PLTL workshops ran alongside traditional lecture halls with fixed seating, providing peer-interactive instruction where the amphitheater setting limited it

citation: Snyder Julia J., Wiles Jason R. (2015). Peer Led Team Learning in Introductory Biology: Effects on Peer Leader Critical Thinking Skills. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0115084
title: Peer-Led Team Learning (PLTL) model as peer-guided small-group problem solving situated in the zone of proximal development
description: PLTL is a pedagogical approach providing small group instruction alongside traditional lecture, in which "students work in small groups of six to eight students led by an undergraduate peer who has previously taken and been successful in the course". Peer leaders are not content experts and do not provide answers; trained in learning theory and pedagogy, they guide students to construct their own understanding. The article frames PLTL with Vygotsky's constructivism: it "situates students in their zone of proximal development by presenting challenging problems that they can't solve easily on their own but can by interacting with peer members of the team", with the peer leader closer to students' ZPD than an instructor.
requirements: Peer leaders must have previously and successfully completed the same course (grade A or B) and be trained in learning theory, pedagogical methods, and course content by the instructor and an education specialist.
Workshops operate without instructor presence, so leaders must facilitate group work rather than supply answers.
constraints: Most prior evidence concerns benefits to workshop students; effects on leaders were under-researched, and this study's null critical-thinking results came from a single first-time implementation at one institution.
target_learners: Undergraduate students in large introductory science lecture courses and the undergraduate peer leaders who facilitate their workshops
examples: The model was originally developed in the early 1990s for undergraduate chemistry courses and later implemented in organic chemistry, biology, and anatomy and physiology.
